turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was aghast, she declared, at the gross misrepresentation of the case, and she had no knowledge whatever of any Lady Bloxham.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was afraid he had been trying to be as honest as possible, Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, her voice dripping with disdain, as she observed, This is a very serious matter indeed, Mr. Worthing, and she was not at all impressed by his candour so far.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: She'd had quite enough of this inquisition, it was time she went in there and put a stop to it, after all, she was the one who was going to be marrying Jack, not Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He couldn't help but wonder, was it really so very serious, what Lady Bracknell seemed to be making of this matter, or was it just, well, a bit of a fuss, perhaps?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was not at all convinced of Jack's suitability as a husband for her daughter, and she found his explanation most unsatisfactory.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He really didn't want to, but he supposed it was only right that he should, well, explain the circumstances of his life a bit further, if Lady Bracknell was so keen to know the truth.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, her voice dripping with disdain, as she declared, This is all quite ridiculous, Mr. Worthing, and she was not at all convinced by his attempts to explain himself.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hoped Lady Bracknell would be willing to listen to the rest of his explanation, as it was really quite a simple matter, really.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's patience was wearing thin, she thought, as she gazed at Jack with a mixture of disdain and incredulity, and she would not rest until he produced some concrete proof of his supposed gentility.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen was growing increasingly impatient, she thought, why was this all taking so long? It was absurd to keep questioning Jack like this, when she had made it quite clear she was perfectly happy with their engagement.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Mr. Worthing, this was all becoming quite too tiresome, he thought, and he daresay he had more important things to attend to than sit here and listen to his vacuous explanations.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hoped Lady Bracknell would see reason and understand that he was not trying to deceive anyone, least of all Gwendolen, whom he loved dearly.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, and she said, 'Really, Mr. Worthing, this is getting quite ridiculous, is it not?'

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, Lady Bracknell, can't you see Jack's perfectly capable of taking care of me, and I'm not some fragile little flower that needs constant supervision.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed, her voice taking on a stern tone as she said, Really, Mr. Worthing, if you cannot produce some satisfactory evidence of your identity, she feared their interview was at an end.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hoped Lady Bracknell would understand that he didn't have any documents to prove his identity, as he had been separated from his guardian, Mr. Septimus, at a very young age.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, she declared that this was preposterous, a young man without any proofs of his identity, and yet he expected to marry a woman of their standing, a connection of hers, and she would not have it.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen was indignant, she protested, that Lady Bracknell could possibly object to Jack's marrying her simply because he didn't have some dusty old papers to prove his identity, a ridiculous and outdated notion, she declared, that a man's worth should be measured by his ability to produce a birth certificate.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was shocked, simply shocked, by Mr. Worthing's lack of proper documents, a most irregular and distressing affair.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
